glossary.note: Windows’ own UI says “This PC” and Microsoft copy says “your PC”. Linux has no brand noun, so “computer”. The biggest single decision: about 60 rows.
glossary.nativeNote: Microsoft copy says “PC”, never “computer”, for the user’s Windows machine.
glossary.source: Windows File Explorer “This PC” node (memory); Microsoft Writing Style Guide uses “PC” (not fetched: learn.microsoft.com is blocked in this session)

glossary.macos: macOS (as the thing that did something)
glossary.note: “macOS blocked…”, “macOS wouldn’t move…”. Linux could say “Linux”, but the refusing layer is often the desktop or a security module, so “the system” is more honest.

Reveal verb: macOS “Show in Finder”, Windows “Show in File Explorer” (VS Code says “Reveal in File Explorer”; Explorer’s own item is “Open file location”), Linux “Show in file manager”. Desktop-specific Linux names need a desktop value or a runtime lookup (`xdg-mime query default inode/directory`).
glossary.nativeNote: Windows users expect “Open file location” / “Show in folder” phrasing as much as the app name; “Show in File Explorer” keeps parity with the Mac label.
glossary.source: Windows 11 context menu “Open file location” (elevenforum.com, windowslatest.com); VS Code label from user reports

glossary.windows: the Recycle Bin (always with “the”, capitalized as the desktop feature)
glossary.linux: Trash (GNOME, KDE en-US); en-GB KDE: Wastebin
glossary.note: Windows’ own delete flow says “Delete” (to the Recycle Bin) and “Permanently delete” (Shift+Delete). Cmdr’s “Move to trash” could become “Delete” on Windows with “Delete permanently” for Shift+F8, which is more native than “Move to Recycle Bin”. The en-GB overlay handles “Bin”/“Wastebin” for Linux if wanted.
glossary.nativeNote: Native Windows phrasing is “Delete” (implies the Recycle Bin) and “Move to the Recycle Bin” only in confirmations; Microsoft capitalizes Recycle Bin for the Windows desktop feature and always writes “the Recycle Bin”.
glossary.source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/a-z-word-list-term-collections/r/recycle-bin (via search summary); KDE en_GB “Wastebin” (bugs.kde.org 379654, Launchpad dolphin en_GB)

glossary.macos: System Settings (+ pane paths, OS-localized via system_strings.rs)
glossary.linux: GNOME: Settings; KDE: System Settings; fallback “your system settings”
glossary.note: Windows paths should be written as Windows writes them; a Windows `system_strings` arm could localize them like macOS’s (ms-settings pages have localized titles).
glossary.nativeNote: Microsoft writes paths as “Settings > Time & language > Date & time” and uses “turn on” for toggles.
glossary.source: Windows Central guide for Settings > Time & language > Date & time

glossary.linux: keyring (GNOME: Passwords and Keys app; KDE: KWallet)
glossary.note: Windows apps almost never name Credential Manager in a checkbox; they say “Remember password”/“Save password”. Name Credential Manager only where the user must go there.
glossary.nativeNote: Windows: “Remember my credentials” / “Remember password” in sign-in dialogs; Credential Manager > Windows Credentials when a user must manage an entry.
glossary.source: GNOME “Passwords and Keys” (Seahorse): en.opensuse.org, flathub.org; Windows from memory

glossary.note: All three Windows/GNOME/KDE say Properties; the permissions tab is “Security” on Windows, “Permissions” on GNOME/KDE.
glossary.nativeNote: Windows: “right-click it and select Properties, then the Security tab” (Microsoft style: “select”, not “choose” or “click”).

glossary.note: Capability-gated; the right answer is hiding, not renaming.
Microsoft Manual of Style: use “exit”, not “quit”, for closing a program; newer guidance prefers “close”. GNOME HIG lists Quit (Ctrl+Q).
glossary.nativeNote: Windows sentences say “Cmdr closed unexpectedly”, “close Cmdr”; the menu item is “Exit”.
glossary.source: Microsoft Manual of Style 4th ed. (oreilly.com summary); developer.gnome.org/hig/reference/keyboard.html

glossary.windows: Terminal (Windows Terminal is the Windows 11 default) with PowerShell syntax
glossary.note: Commands differ more than the noun: `ls -la`/`df -h`/`lsof` don’t exist in PowerShell; `ping` does. Each Windows row uses a Windows command or a GUI route.
glossary.nativeNote: Windows users rarely get command-line advice; a GUI route (Properties > Security, Task Manager) is the native first step.

glossary.linux: system monitor (GNOME: System Monitor, KDE: System Monitor)
GNOME: Disks (Check Filesystem); KDE: KDE Partition Manager
glossary.nativeNote: Windows calls it error checking; the button is “Check”.

glossary.note: Dock strings are capability-gated; this matters only for the desktop-wide “empty the Trash in the Dock” advice.
Microsoft docs say “the drive where Windows is installed (usually C:)” and “system drive”.

strings.currentEnglish:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click it, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to see the current permissions
strings.description: Recovery suggestion for a no-permission read (errno path). Markdown bullet list. `{system_settings}`, `{privacy_and_security}`, `{files_and_folders}` are do-not-translate placeholders replaced at runtime with OS-localized pane names. "Get Info" and "Sharing & Permissions" are Finder labels that Apple localizes, so use your locale's Finder wording for both. Same for the app names "Finder" and "Terminal": use whatever your locale's macOS calls them (most keep the English name; zh-Hans does not). The backtick command is literal; do NOT translate it.

strings.currentEnglish:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by moving or deleting files you no longer need
- Empty the Trash (right-click the Trash icon in the Dock)
- In Terminal, run `df -h` to see how much space is left on each volume
- Check **{system_settings} > General > Storage** for a breakdown of what’s using space
strings.description: Recovery suggestion for a full disk (errno path). Markdown bullet list. `{system_settings}` is a do-not-translate placeholder replaced at runtime with the System Settings app name as the USER'S MAC shows it, whatever language Cmdr itself runs in. Keep it verbatim, and never attach a case suffix or article directly to it (Hungarian "{system_settings}ben"): the runtime value is unknown, so restructure the sentence instead. The pane names the snapshot doesn't resolve ("General", "Storage") are ordinary copy: use the wording macOS shows for them in your language. "Dock" and the backtick command are literal; do NOT translate. "Trash" is the macOS Trash: use your language's settled term for it. "Terminal" is Apple's app: use the name your language's macOS shows for it (most keep the English name, Chinese doesn't; check the reference pile or the app bundle).

strings.currentEnglish:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click the folder, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the path to see the current permissions
strings.description: Recovery suggestion for a no-permission read (typed variant). Markdown bullet list. `{system_settings}`, `{privacy_and_security}`, `{files_and_folders}` are do-not-translate placeholders replaced at runtime with OS-localized pane names. "Get Info" and "Sharing & Permissions" are Finder labels that Apple localizes, so use your locale's Finder wording for both. Same for the app names "Finder" and "Terminal": use whatever your locale's macOS calls them (most keep the English name; zh-Hans does not). The backtick command is literal; do NOT translate it.

strings.currentEnglish: macOS is still using something there. Wait a minute, then try again.
strings.description: Shown when the only thing holding the drive is macOS itself (Spotlight indexing it, Time Machine, and so on). There's nothing for the person to close, so the advice is to wait rather than to hunt for an app. "macOS" is Apple's product name: keep it exactly as written, and don't translate it. Surface: a brief error toast in the top-right of Cmdr's main window, shown after someone asks to eject a drive or disconnect a network share. Your string is dropped into "Couldn't eject {volumeName}: …" or "Couldn't disconnect: …", so it reads as the sentence AFTER a colon; every errors.eject.* string starts with a capital letter, as a full sentence; if your language lowercases after a colon, do it for the whole errors.eject.* family, never for one key alone. No surface shows it on its own (only Cmdr’s toasts read it). The same sentence follows both, and the lead-in already says which action it was and what it was done to, so name neither: no "drive", no "share", no "eject" or "disconnect". Point at the place with a plain "there" and ask to "try again". Plain text, one or two short sentences, no markdown. Cmdr never uses the words "error" or "failed" in messages people read.
strings.whereInUi: Toast after Eject fails (volume switcher eject button or its row menu) because a system process holds the drive.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: The holder list comes from macOS’s DiskArbitration dissenter today; the Linux and Windows eject paths don’t report holders.

strings.currentEnglish: “{server}” is answering, but macOS’s network sign-in helper looks stuck, so no share can connect right now. To restart it, open Terminal, run killall NetAuthSysAgent, then try again. macOS starts the helper again on its own.
strings.description: Shown when a network share (SMB) waited a long time without connecting while the server itself is reachable: a macOS background helper called NetAuthSysAgent is stuck, and only restarting it helps. Surface: the network pane, after someone opens a shared folder on a network server. The pane replaces the server's list of shares with a "Couldn't mount share" title, this text under it, and Try again and Back buttons. "Network sign-in helper" isn't a name macOS shows anywhere: it describes a nameless background process, so describe it in your language's words (a service or a process). Keep "killall NetAuthSysAgent" exactly as written, untranslated: it's a command the person types into Terminal. "Terminal" is the macOS app's name; use the name macOS shows for it in your language. Plain text, no markdown. Cmdr never uses the words "error" or "failed" in messages people read.
strings.whereInUi: Toast or sign-in sheet message when mounting an SMB share hangs in macOS’s NetAuthSysAgent.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: NetAuthSysAgent is a macOS daemon; the reason is produced only by the macOS mount path.

strings.currentEnglish: Unlock it in Finder (Get Info > uncheck Locked) and try again.  ‖  [errors.write.fileLocked.suggestion.other] The file may be protected. Check its permissions (e.g. via chmod or your file manager) and try again.
strings.description: Recovery suggestion for a locked file on macOS. Plain text. Apple localizes both "Get Info" (the Finder menu command) and "Locked" (the checkbox in its Info window), so write the menu path with your locale's Finder wording. "Finder" is the app name: use whatever your locale's macOS calls it.  ‖  [errors.write.fileLocked.suggestion.other] Recovery suggestion for a locked file on non-macOS. Plain text. "chmod" is a command name; do NOT translate it.
strings.whereInUi: Transfer error dialog (TransferErrorDialog) that opens when a copy, move, delete, or move to trash stops on an item; advice under “File is locked” when a delete hits a locked file.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Picked by `isMacOS()` at the call site. The `.other` half says “Check its permissions (e.g. via chmod or your file manager)”: `chmod` is meaningless on Windows, “e.g.” breaks the style of the rest, and on Windows the locking flag is the Read-only attribute in Properties.
strings.macos: Unlock it in Finder (Get Info > uncheck Locked) and try again.
strings.windows: The file may be read-only. In File Explorer, open its Properties, clear **Read-only**, and try again.
strings.linux: The file may be protected. Check its permissions in your file manager, or with `chmod` in a terminal, and try again.

linuxDesktops.gnome: The file may be protected. Check its permissions in Files, or with `chmod` in a terminal, and try again.
linuxDesktops.kde: The file may be protected. Check its permissions in Dolphin, or with `chmod` in Konsole, and try again.
linuxDesktops.fallback: The file may be protected. Check its permissions in your file manager, or with `chmod` in a terminal, and try again.

strings.icu: {platform, select, macos {Unlock it in Finder (Get Info > uncheck Locked) and try again.} windows {The file may be read-only. In File Explorer, open its Properties, clear **Read-only**, and try again.} other {The file may be protected. Check its permissions in your file manager, or with `chmod` in a terminal, and try again.}}   (illustrative: raw family, ships as `<key>.windows` / `<key>.linux` siblings)
strings.nativeNote: Windows users expect “Open file location” / “Show in folder” phrasing as much as the app name; “Show in File Explorer” keeps parity with the Mac label. Windows: “right-click it and select Properties, then the Security tab” (Microsoft style: “select”, not “choose” or “click”).
strings.implementationNote: Collapses the pair into ONE key (`errors.write.fileLocked.suggestion`) with platform variants via the raw-family mechanism; delete `.mac`/`.other` and the `isMacOS()` branch. Does the backend produce `file_locked` off macOS? Lock flags are read only on macOS today, so the Linux/Windows halves are future-proofing.

"Cmdr" is the product name and "SMB" a protocol name; keep both.

strings.currentEnglish: Runs a small language model entirely on your device. Maximum privacy: nothing leaves your computer. Works offline. Uses ~2 GB disk space and ~400 MB memory (varies with context size). Requires Apple silicon (M1+) and macOS 14 or later.

"~2 GB" and "~400 MB" are rough decimal sizes: keep the tilde and write the units as your common.sizeUnit.gigabyte and common.sizeUnit.megabyte. "M1" is an Apple chip name; keep it. "Apple silicon" is Apple’s name for its own M-series Mac chips: use the form your language’s termbase settles, since Apple frames it in its own words in some languages. "M1+" means M1 or later. "context size" ties to the local context-window setting.

strings.whyItNeedsWork: Every OS shows the provider picker. “Requires Apple silicon (M1+) and macOS 14 or later” is a hard requirement, so on Windows/Linux the option is always disabled; the tooltip should say it’s Mac-only rather than list Mac specs.

strings.currentEnglish: Undo move to trash of {countText} items
strings.description: VERB phrase (imperative). The menu.edit.undoTrash item once the user has moved TWO OR MORE files or folders to the trash in one go, so the item says how many it would put back. The command palette shows the same words. The native menu can't pick a plural form, so {countText} is always 2 or more: if your language inflects the noun differently across numbers of 2 and up, use a shape that reads right for every one of them (like "items: {countText}"). Use the same trash term as menu.edit.undoTrash. Keep the {countText} token exactly as written, braces included; it is replaced literally.
strings.whereInUi: Same Edit menu row once several items were trashed.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Move to trash is on every OS (Linux today, Windows next). Windows names the place “the Recycle Bin”, so “trash” as noun or verb reads foreign there.

strings.currentEnglish: Minimize
strings.description: VERB (imperative). macOS Window-menu item that sends the window down to the Dock (⌘M). Use the exact word macOS uses for Minimize in this language; this menu is one users read as system-standard.

strings.currentEnglish: Eject ({name})
strings.description: VERB (imperative). Right-click item on a disk in the path bar or the volume dropdown: safely unmounts it so it can be unplugged. Use the exact word your macOS Finder uses for Eject. Keep the {name} token exactly as written, braces included; it is replaced literally, with no formatting, and can be any length. Its busy form is menu.volume.ejectBusy.

strings.whyItNeedsWork: Windows File Explorer says “Eject” for removable drives and mounted images; GNOME says “Eject” or “Unmount”. Neutral. Neutral here because Windows, GNOME, and KDE use this same word in their own UI, not as a cross-platform compromise.

strings.currentEnglish: Keep Cmdr in your Dock?
strings.description: Title of a one-time notification, shown a few days into using Cmdr on macOS, asking whether the app may add itself to the Dock. The Dock is the row of app icons along the edge of a macOS screen; use the name Apple uses for it in your language. "Cmdr" is the product name and stays verbatim. A genuine question, warm and low-pressure, never a prompt the user has to escape from.

strings.whyItNeedsWork: Gated by `dockPin` (NUDGE_CAPABILITY).
strings.macos: Keep Cmdr in your Dock?

strings.currentEnglish: You’ve been using Cmdr for a few days now, so it seems to be working for you. Want it pinned next to Finder down there?
strings.description: Body of that notification. Two beats: the app noticed the person keeps coming back, and the offer itself. "Finder" is Apple's file manager and keeps the name Apple uses in your language; "pinned" means the icon stays in the Dock even when the app is closed. "a few days" is deliberately vague and must NOT be replaced with a number: the exact threshold can move. "down there" points at the Dock, which usually sits at the bottom of the screen; drop the direction if it would be wrong or odd in your language.
strings.whereInUi: Same Dock toast, body.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Gated by `dockPin`.

strings.currentEnglish: Cmdr needs a newer Safari
strings.description: Heading of the full-screen notice Cmdr shows instead of its interface when the Mac's WebKit is too old to run the app at all. It replaces the whole window, so this is the first and only thing the person sees. "Cmdr" is the product name and stays untranslated; "Safari" is Apple's browser and keeps whatever name Apple uses in the target language. Cmdr's interface is drawn by the system WebKit, which tracks the Safari version, so "a newer Safari" is literally what is needed. Keep it short: it is a heading.
strings.whereInUi: Boot-guard screen when the WebKit is too old (app.html).
strings.whyItNeedsWork: The guard exists for old Safari/WKWebView. On Windows (WebView2, evergreen) and Linux (WebKitGTK) a too-old engine reads very differently.
strings.macos: Cmdr needs a newer Safari
strings.question: Could the guard fire on Linux with an old WebKitGTK? Then Linux needs “Cmdr needs a newer WebKitGTK; update your system” wording.

"Software Update" is the macOS system settings pane: use the name Apple uses for it in the target language, since the person has to find it. "15.4" is a Safari version number and stays as digits. "Cmdr" is the product name and stays untranslated. Tone is calm and practical, not an apology: this is fixable by installing pending macOS updates, and on most old Macs it is.

strings.whyItNeedsWork: See title.

It names the version the person is actually on so the message reads as being about THEIR Mac, not a generic warning. "Cmdr" is the product name and "macOS" is Apple's OS name; both stay untranslated. It is a statement, not a warning or an apology: the app is running fine, and the body explains the caveats.

strings.currentEnglish: Cmdr officially supports macOS 12 and up, so here it’s best effort. Most of it works, but some colors and small layout details can look off, and fixes for older systems come last. If you hit something broken, I’d still like to hear about it.
strings.description: Body of the one-time old-macOS dialog under main.oldMacos.title, shown once per machine and never again. Three things, in order: this macOS is outside the tested range, what that costs in practice (some colors and small layout details can be wrong), and an invitation to report anything broken anyway. "12" is a macOS version number and stays as digits. "Best effort" means Cmdr tries but makes no promises here; use whatever phrase carries that in the target language rather than a literal rendering. "Come last" means such fixes are the lowest priority, not that they never happen. The last sentence is Cmdr's maker speaking in the first person, which is deliberate; keep it warm and personal, and use the informal register if the language has one. Tone throughout is honest and relaxed, NOT an apology and NOT a warning.
strings.whereInUi: Same notice, body.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Same.

strings.currentEnglish: If you enable this, Cmdr can connect to Android phones, Kindles, cameras, some music players, and any other device that supports the protocols called MTP or PTP. The cost is that macOS also wants to connect to these (and it usually fails, which is why you can’t just use Finder to copy photos from Android phones), so Cmdr has to suppress that macOS process while it’s running. When you quit Cmdr, this is politely restored.
strings.description: The long MTP explanation, shown in the tooltip behind the info glyph: it lets the app talk to phones, e-readers, and cameras, at the cost of temporarily suppressing a conflicting macOS process, which is put back on quit. <strong> bolds the device list; <em> emphasizes "also". "Cmdr" is the product name; "macOS" is the operating system; "Finder" is the macOS file manager; "Android", "Kindles", "MTP", and "PTP" are device/protocol names; all stay untranslated. Each sentence sits on its own line (the newlines are real line breaks in the tooltip); keep one line per sentence in your translation.
strings.whereInUi: Same step, MTP row detail.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Explains that macOS competes for the device (ptpcamerad) and that Finder can’t show it; neither holds on Windows (MTP ships on Windows via WPD) or Linux (GVFS may grab it).

strings.currentEnglish: Something on this Mac is keeping Cmdr from connecting to {server} directly, so this share stays on the system connection. Try switching Cmdr off and on under {localNetwork}, or check your firewall app.
strings.description: Toast and notification body shown when Cmdr's own faster connection to a network share was refused by something on the user's Mac, while macOS's own connection to the same server works. The usual cause is the macOS Local Network privacy permission for Cmdr being stuck (it shows as on, and switching it off and on fixes it), or a firewall app. Reassures the user that the share still works, just not at the faster speed. A button below it opens that permission's page in System Settings ("openLocalNetworkSettings"). "Cmdr" is the product name; "firewall app" means third-party firewall software such as Little Snitch or LuLu.
strings.whereInUi: Toast on an SMB share when Cmdr’s direct connection is blocked locally (firewall or Local Network permission), so the share stays on the OS mount.
strings.whyItNeedsWork: The reason comes from macOS’s Local Network refusal (EHOSTUNREACH under TCC); the `{localNetwork}` token is a macOS pane. A Windows firewall block would be a new reason with its own copy.
strings.macos: Something on this Mac is keeping Cmdr from connecting to {server} directly, so this share stays on the system connection. Try switching Cmdr off and on under {localNetwork}, or check your firewall app.
strings.translationImpact: None. Optionally add “Shown on macOS only” to the @key description so translators can use Apple’s localized terms freely.

The known cause: macOS keeps Cmdr's Local Network privacy permission tied to the old version, so it shows as on but doesn't apply; switching it off and on in System Settings fixes it at once. A button below it opens that permission's page ("openLocalNetworkSettings"), and another retries the connection. Reassures the user that the share still works, just slower. "Cmdr" is the product name.

strings.currentEnglish: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>. You are connected, but only via macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is 4x slower for most connections (sometimes 100x) than Cmdr’s direct connection. Click the button below to try again.
strings.description: Body of the notification that appears when Cmdr couldn’t open its own faster connection to a network share, so the share is running on the connection macOS provides. It explains the speed cost and points at the button below it (the "osMountFallback.retry" key). <shareName> wraps the share’s name and renders it bold; keep the tag around the name wherever your grammar puts it. "4x" and "100x" are speed multipliers; write them the way your language writes multipliers. "macOS", "SMB", and "Cmdr" are names; keep them.
strings.whereInUi: Toast on an SMB share when Cmdr fell back to the OS’s own SMB mount (shares mounted by the system).
strings.whyItNeedsWork: Linux has an OS mount too (GVFS), so this can fire there and says “macOS’s native SMB network connection”. Windows’ equivalent is its own SMB client (mapped drive).

strings.currentEnglish: Some of your selection is online-only. Moving those to the Trash would download them first. In this case, Cmdr only offers to delete the entire selection. There’ll be no copies in the Trash, but cloud services usually keep their own trash for about 30 days. Click “Delete” if deletion is OK, otherwise cancel this dialog and either make all files available offline first, or deselect all online-only files.
strings.description: Warning banner in the delete dialog, shown when the person pressed the "move to trash" key over a selection where SOME items are online-only and the rest aren't. Online-only means the file lives in a cloud-storage folder (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, …) and the provider has evicted its contents to its own servers, leaving a placeholder on the Mac; "online-only" is Apple's Finder term, so prefer your platform's own existing wording for it. Four facts, all of which matter: (1) the Trash lives on the Mac, so putting an online-only file there would download it from the cloud service first; (2) because one gesture can't be half a trash and half a delete, Cmdr offers to delete the WHOLE selection permanently; (3) there will be NO copies in the macOS Trash afterwards, though the cloud service keeps its own deleted-files history (Dropbox keeps 30 days) to restore from — don't soften this into "it goes to the trash anyway", it does not; (4) two ways out, both real in Cmdr: make the files available offline (the provider's own download action, in Cmdr's right-click menu — don't name that menu item, its label comes from the provider), or deselect the online-only files (Cmdr badges them in the file pane). <strong> bolds "download them first" and "delete". “Delete” in quotes is the confirm button's own label: use the same word you translated fileOperations.delete.confirmDelete to. "Click" is deliberate even though Enter works too. "Trash" is the macOS Trash the Finder uses; the lowercase "their own trash" is the cloud service's, not Apple's.

strings.description: Note above the search results about folders macOS's privacy protection kept Cmdr out of, so their contents are missing from the results. These are the ones Full Disk Access opens: when Cmdr doesn't have that permission yet, the offer below (search.coverage.deniedFullDiskAccess) follows. 'macOS' is the operating system's name and stays as-is. It's one line: the folder paths sit in a tooltip behind the icon before it, and a copy button after it copies them all. The English singular branch reads 'one folder'; in languages whose 'one' category also covers other numbers, put that wording in an =1 branch. The line only appears when at least one folder is affected, so 0 never reaches it. Avoid the words 'error' and 'failed'.

strings.whyItNeedsWork: Every OS can deny a folder; Linux reads “macOS didn’t let Cmdr look inside…”.

strings.currentEnglish: {host} is answering, but macOS’s network sign-in helper looks stuck. To restart it, open Terminal, run killall NetAuthSysAgent, then try again. macOS starts the helper again on its own.
strings.description: Shown in the pane when a saved network share (SMB) waited a long time without connecting while the server itself is reachable: a macOS background helper called NetAuthSysAgent is stuck, and only restarting it helps. “Network sign-in helper” isn’t a name macOS shows anywhere: it describes a nameless background process, so describe it in your language’s words (a service or a process). mechanismOptions.title: Inject `platform` into every ICU format call (recommended)
mechanismOptions.how: In `apps/desktop/src/lib/intl/messages.svelte.ts`, `t()` (line ~441) and `tStringIn()` (~482) call `getCompiled(locale, key).format(params)`; pass `{ platform: getPlatform(), ...params }` instead, and `Trans.svelte` builds its handler object the same way. `getPlatform()` from `#lib/platform` reads `window.__CMDR_PLATFORM__` per call, so the compiled-message cache (keyed by locale and key) stays valid and `withPlatform()` in tests flips the branch without cache busting. Messages then write `{platform, select, macos {…} windows {…} other {…}}`; `other` is Linux and every fallback context (Vitest, plain browser), matching `FALLBACK_PLATFORM = 'linux'`.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: Pros: one key per string, translators see all variants together, no call-site changes, the existing `.mac`/`.other` pairs collapse. Cons: `platform` becomes a reserved param name (a caller passing its own `platform` must be a type error: make `TranslationParams` exclude it); `#lib/platform` is a new import of the runtime (allowed: it reads a global, no logger/settings); messages with nested `plural`/`select` get longer.
checks: i18n-parity: `platform` counts as a placeholder; every locale must keep the SAME branch set English has (`macos`, `windows`, `other`), not just the arg. New rule, since parity today compares only placeholder names.

i18n-coverage: today’s SOURCE-TEXT-ONLY logic flags a value whose branches differ from English only by category; teach it that a `platform` select copied with English text in one branch is still untranslated (it already warns per branch; make the windows/other branch count).
i18n-plural: unaffected, but must recurse into each platform branch (it already walks nested ICU).

New `i18n-platform-select`: `platform` may only appear as a top-level select (no `{platform}` interpolation, so no OS name leaks as raw text), branches limited to `macos | windows | linux | other`, `other` required.
New ESLint `cmdr/no-platform-copy-branch`: forbid `isMacOS() ? tString(a) : tString(b)` and `{#if isMacOS()}` around copy; the ~10 remaining copy call sites go away.
desktop-message-keys-unused: the collapsed `.mac`/`.other` keys disappear, so their allowlist entries (if any) go too.
i18n-dont-translate / quoted-labels: branch-aware, so “Finder” is expected only in the macos branch and a quoted label (“Remember password”) is matched per branch.

mechanismOptions.title: Raw families (`errors.*`, Rust `menu.*`): a top-level platform block, resolved before the raw pipeline (recommended)
mechanismOptions.how: Both raw paths can’t use ICU (`getMessage()` + `expandSystemStrings` + snarkdown; Rust `menu_t` is lookup + `.replace`). Allow ONE construct: a value that is entirely `{platform, select, macos {…} windows {…} other {…}}`, whose branch bodies stay raw. A ~40-line splitter (shared by `getMessage()`, the native-strings generator, and the checks) picks the branch first; everything after is unchanged. For Rust, `pnpm intl:native-strings` resolves the block at generation time into per-target tables selected by `cfg(target_os)`, so `menu_t` stays a lookup and `crates/cmdr-menu`’s `PerPlatform<&str>` (macos/linux only today) can retire its two-key labels.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: Pros: translators see one string with variants in every family; no new keys; Rust needs no ICU. Cons: a second, tiny grammar to keep in sync with ICU’s (mitigated by sharing one splitter and making `i18n-icu` validate the block shape for raw keys). Alternative M2b: platform-suffixed sibling keys (`errors.x.suggestion.windows`) with a `key.<platform>` → `key` fallback; simpler parser-wise, but doubles keys, needs the unused-key and parity checks to learn sibling groups, and translators see variants apart. Alternative M2c: move `errors.*` to ICU; rejected by the runtime’s own reasons (snarkdown/esc/`{system_settings}` collisions).

mechanismOptions.title: OS-supplied names (`system_strings.rs`) per platform
mechanismOptions.how: `{system_settings}`, `{privacy_and_security}`, `{localNetwork}`, `{appearance}` resolve to macOS pane names from `.loctable` files; off macOS they fall back to the English MAC defaults (so Linux shows “System Settings” today). Give `LocalizedSystemStrings` per-OS arms: Windows could read localized Settings page titles (or ship English “Settings” defaults), Linux returns desktop names. Most token users are capability-gated (FDA, Local Network); for the few that aren’t, the platform select carries a Windows path and the tokens stay in the macos branch.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: Keeps OS-localized pane names on macOS; avoids pretending Windows/Linux have the same panes. Low priority once the ungated Local Network block is gated.

mechanismOptions.title: Linux desktop value (later)
mechanismOptions.how: Rows carry `linuxDesktops` (GNOME/KDE/fallback). Shipping them needs a `desktop` value beside `platform` (from `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP`, injected by the same init script) and a nested select in the `other` branch: `other {{desktop, select, gnome {Show in Files} kde {Show in Dolphin} other {Show in file manager}}}`. For the file manager specifically, `code` is better: read the default `inode/directory` handler’s display name at runtime and pass it as `{fileManager}`.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: Native names on the two big desktops at the cost of 2 more branches per string for translators. Recommend shipping the fallback first and adding `desktop` only for the ~15 highest-traffic rows (reveal, trash, settings paths, keyring).

mechanismOptions.title: Shortcut glyphs in prose → placeholders
mechanismOptions.how: The 8 values with literal ⌘/⌥/⌃/⇧ become `{combo}` placeholders (or self-closing `<key></key>` tags) filled from `getEffectiveShortcuts(id)` + `formatKeyCombo`, as `fileExplorer.quickLookHint` already does. One English string for all platforms, and user rebinds show correctly.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: Needs task 26’s per-platform keymap to be right first; each locale re-translates once.

mechanismOptions.title: Browser demo, tests, golden fixtures
mechanismOptions.how: The demo defines `__CMDR_PLATFORM__` from the visitor’s UA (`lib/demo/platform.ts`), so a Windows visitor gets the windows branch automatically. Vitest defaults to `'linux'` → the `other` branch: every test asserting a Mac string must add `withPlatform('macos')`, which is the point. The frozen `#lib/error-messages/__fixtures__/friendly_error_golden.json` (“never regenerate”) must be asserted under `withPlatform('macos')`, and gains sibling goldens for windows/linux. The i18n screenshot run (`pnpm i18n:shots`, macOS) can’t photograph windows/linux branches; the `@key.screenshot` field needs a per-platform form or an explicit “no screenshot for this branch” marker.
mechanismOptions.tradeoffs: None real; just budget for the test sweep (expect a few hundred assertions to touch).

Translations already carry macOS vocabulary where English is neutral (de `menu.window.minimize` “Im Dock ablegen”, ru “Убрать в Dock”); 370 `@key` descriptions tell translators to use “the word your language’s macOS uses”. Task 28 needs a translator-brief rule: in a platform select, each branch uses that OS’s own localized term, and descriptions of keys shown off macOS get reworded.

Unverified behavior that decides wording: Windows firewall prompt for SMB discovery, MTP exclusivity on Windows (WPD vs libmtp), the WebDAV trust store off macOS, whether the global download shortcut works on Wayland/Windows, Windows hidden-file rule (attribute vs dot), whether Go to path accepts `~` on Windows.
readMe: Each row is one string (or one existing .mac/.other pair, keys joined by “ + ”). `macos` is today’s text unless `macosChanged`. `windows`/`linux` are proposals; `linuxDesktops` gives GNOME/KDE wording where they differ, with `fallback` = `linux`. Mechanism `select` is the default (platform-native wording per OS); `neutral` only where all three OSes’ own UIs say the same; `none` = macOS-only by capability or backend; `split-feature` = hide or redesign; `code` = the text comes from runtime data (shortcut, app name). `rawFamily` rows (errors.*, menu.*) can’t use ICU today; their `icu` is illustrative (see mechanismOptions M2). Vocabulary sources that couldn’t be fetched are `verified: false` in the glossary.
